newsitem.title: USA: Okla. City bomb suspects can face death penalty.
newsitem.headline: Okla. City bomb suspects can face death penalty.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial rejected various defence arguments and cleared the way on Wednesday for the two defendants in the case to face the death penalty if convicted.

U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch rejected a number of defence arguments, including one that Justice Department lawyers did not follow proper procedures when they decided to seek the death penalty.

Timothy McVeigh and his former army buddy Terry Nichols were expected to be tried later this year or early 1997 in Denver for the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that claimed the lives of 168 and injured hundreds more.
The decision was an important one for prosecutors. "This clears the way for us to seek the death penalty. It mows down all the challenges," said Leesa Brown, spokeswoman for the Justice Department.

Defence attorneys said proper procedures were not followed when Attorney General Janet Reno said the death penalty would be sought even before the arrest of the two men. Other objections, including the argument that the death penalty represents cruel and unusual punishment, were also rejected.
Stephen Jones, McVeigh's attorney, said Wednesday's decision was not a surprise because trial judges are "very reluctant" to strike down the dealth penalty before a trial gets underway.
"It does not change our strategy," he said and if his client is convicted "we are prepared to argue the death penalty should not be imposed" because of mitigating circumstances.
The trial was moved to Denver after Matsch ruled the two defendants could not receive a fair hearing anywhere in Oklahoma.
A pre-trial hearing was scheduled for next week to hear defence arguments on whether McVeigh and Nichols should be tried together.
Earlier this year Matsch dismissed a civil lawsuit brought by Nichols against Reno over the death penalty. Wednesday's decision dealt with the issue on the criminal level.
